newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK-Reforms on the agenda, again.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK-Reforms on the agenda, again.

text.p: The Brazilian government, hoping to make up for lost time on key pieces of legislation, will seek to put several important bills to votes in Congress this week, officials said Monday.

Top of the agenda of an extraordinary session running through the July recess are the government's reforms of the civil serivce, currently stuck in the Chamber of Deputies, and of the pension system which is awaiting a Senate panel vote.

The civil service reform bill itself was approved on the lower house floor in April, two years after being sent to Congress. But the government has yet to pluck up the courage to vote on some crucial amendments which threaten to make a mockery of the reform.

As they have done for nearly two months, government whips told newspapers over the weekend the time had finally come to try and defeat a crucial amendment which would allow civil servants to hang on to their lifetime job guarantees.

The whips fear they will not muster the three-fifths majority needed to kill the proposal because many lawmakers enjoy the backing of a civil service lobby or are worried about losing votes in next year's elections if they back job cuts.
Another fiscally expensive opposition amendment which could be voted this week seeks to maintain rules which entitle civil service pensioners to any pay rise awarded to workers.

Once the amendments have been approved -- and optimistic government whips say that process might be completed this week -- the civil service reform bill faces a second, full vote in the Chamber of Deputies before moving to the Senate.

No real progress is expected this week on the pension reform bill. The government is under pressure to allow civil servants to keep some perks and is only likely to put the bill to a vote in its Senate committee next week.
An important bill facing a vote in the Chamber of Deputies this week would extend the government's Fiscal Stabilization Fund (FEF) until 1999.

The FEF enables the National Treasury to keep about $25 billion a year earmarked for local governments. The money is used to cover holes in the federal budget before the remainder is given to states and municipalities.

The new version of the fund proposes to steadily reduce the impact on the budgets of municipalities. But hundreds of mayors are expected to come to Brasilia Tuesday to lobby for more money before the bill is voted.
As a constitutional amendment, it needs two three-fifths majorities before moving to the Senate.
Also in the lower house, a bill outlining the rules of next year's presidential, congressional and state governorship elections was scheduled for a first, committee-level vote.

The bill is likely to spark a political battle between the government and some of its allied parties. They may not challenge the re-election bid of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, but will want to limit the scope for use of the "state machine" by state governors in the run-up to October 1998.
In the upper house, two bills to open Brazil's huge oil and telecommunications sectors to private competition are up for votes this week.

Three Senate committees were scheduled to vote simultaneously Tuesday on a bill regulating the privatization of the telecommunications industry. Government whips were also expected to put forward a motion which would allow the bill to be put to full and final vote on the Senate floor Thursday.

And a bill setting down the details of how private companies may operate in Brazil's oil and gas industries was due to be put to a vote in the Senate's Economic Affairs Committee Tuesday. If approved there, the legislation goes to another committee before reaching the floor of the Senate.
